Software Engineering.title: Superintelligent Software Engineering: Governance That Scales with Capability
Software Engineering.summary: Software agents are being trained to exceed human engineers; we argue that capability alone does not produce better software engineering. We define superintelligent software engineering as the discipline of building and evolving software with agents whose capability exceeds that of human engineers, in which governance (gates, contracts, decisions and decay control) scales with capability. The argument rests on three claims. First, correctness in a project rests on decisions and contracts that the code does not carry. Second, knowledge decays. Third, once an agent outpaces its reviewers, reading catches a shrinking share of the changes built on stale knowledge. A simple model shows that, past a fixed review capacity, escaping changes grow linearly with throughput while the share that reading catches falls toward zero; governance can lower the slope, capability alone cannot. An exploratory snapshot of 452 of the most-starred public GitHub repositories finds a root-level or .github agent context file in 48.67% (95% confidence interval 44.1 to 53.3); in the median file that names repository paths, 9.5% to 22% of those paths do not resolve, depending on how a reference is read. We then present OSTEON, a discipline for the regime, released with a DOI (10.5281/zenodo.23436020): each project gets a governed knowledge repository of decisions and contracts, every change is checked mechanically against it, and the knowledge itself is checked for decay at every session start; planning is gated, and sessions record what they learn without writing rules. We report no measured effect of OSTEON, mark claims about its mechanisms as opinion and the author's practice heuristics as design rationale, and state the questions that would falsify the thesis.
Software Engineering.comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Collection scripts and dataset are provided as ancillary files. The OSTEON artifact is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23436020

Software Engineering.title: Beyond Accuracy: Disentangling Decomposition from Typed-State Quality Assurance in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
Software Engineering.summary: Multi-agent LLM pipelines are often credited with gains in software engineering tasks, but it is rarely clear whether a gain stems from the typed contract between agents or from the specialized prompts that decomposition enables. We study this attribution problem in Requirements Engineering, comparing three architectures for classifying requirements as functional or non-functional and then prioritizing them with MoSCoW: a single-call baseline; a two-call variant that reuses the pipeline's specialized prompts but passes an unvalidated intermediate; and a pipeline with a Pydantic-validated typed state. The 18 conditions cover PROMISE NFR+ (625 requirements), three locally hosted small language models, and two languages. The F1 gain over the baseline is associated with the two-call, specialized-prompt variant (up to +0.075), whereas the typed state adds a small difference (-0.003 to +0.013) that is significant in one of six comparisons. Beyond accuracy, the typed pipeline contains out-of-range model outputs at the agent boundary, while the unvalidated variant fails later and drops the requirement, and it shows a small, reproducible increase in inter-model MoSCoW consistency whose cause our design cannot isolate. The study is associative: the contrasts bundle prompts, call count, and staged context, and the results come from three 7--8B models on one dataset. The implementation and replication package are archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23380444).
Software Engineering.comment: 10 pages, 10 tables. To be published at Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality -- Simpósio Brasileiro de Qualidade de Software (SBQS)

Software Engineering.title: DynamiQ: Unlocking the Potential of Dynamic Task Allocation in Parallel Fuzzing
Software Engineering.summary: We present DynamiQ, a full-fledged and optimized successor to AFLTeam that supports dynamic and adaptive parallel fuzzing. Unlike most existing approaches that treat individual seeds as tasks, DynamiQ leverages structural information from the program's call graph to define tasks and continuously refines task allocation using runtime feedback. This design significantly reduces redundant exploration and enhances fuzzing efficiency at scale. Built on top of the state-of-the-art LibAFL framework, DynamiQ incorporates several practical optimizations in both task allocation and task-aware fuzzing. We evaluate DynamiQ on eighteen targets from Magma and FuzzBench with a total budget of over 40 CPU years. It achieves the highest mean branch coverage on fourteen targets, with average relative gains ranging from 8.37% to 19.53% over five baseline fuzzers. Across our experiments, DynamiQ identifies nine previously unknown bugs.

Software Engineering.title: ProductWebBench: Evaluating Website Continuity Beyond Task Completion
Software Engineering.summary: Frontend coding agents are usually graded on one question: did the requested target get built. Real engineering changes carry a second obligation, because the rest of the site has to keep working. We call that second obligation website continuity, and introduce ProductWebBench, a benchmark that scores both on living frontend repositories: 320 Change tasks over existing code and 80 long-horizon Build tasks. Every task freezes a repository snapshot, staged requirements, browser evidence and deterministic checks before evaluation, and enters only once a reference passes every check and plausible-wrong ones fail. A simulated user reveals the requirements one stage at a time, and every check cleared earlier stays armed for the rest of the run. Across 8,737 runs from 13 models the two come apart: of the Change runs passing every requested-work check, 28.2% still fail a continuity check -- a blank route, horizontal overflow, console errors -- and 10.8% push a browser state they had already passed back to failing. Because the same checks also run on the untouched repository, each regression carries exact provenance, not a post-hoc label: on the 586 runs where both readings exist, 18.3% are caught breaking a verified state. Interaction is a further blind spot, failing in 29.5% of runs whose static DOM already passes. ProductWebBench therefore scores a patch against the living system it lands in, not the target alone.
Software Engineering.comment: 35 pages, including appendix

Software Engineering.title: Operator Packages, Proposer Strength, and Construction-Family Plateaus in Office-Scale Verified Search
Software Engineering.summary: Verified search, in which a language model proposes programs, a hard evaluator scores them, and selection keeps the best, has recently moved mathematical records; controlled ablations of the proposer-side components remain rare. We instrument a minimal FunSearch-style loop at office scale (a 30B local model on a laptop, 120-600 verified samples per run) with three operator packages: a schematic notebook the model writes and carries instead of verbatim elites, a named obstacle, and behavioural repulsion from constructions already found. On nine construction problems from a public repository, the complete 2^3 factorial with two replicates favours the primary contrast in a nominal two-stage analysis: the composition closes more of the seed-to-record gap (+0.196; nominal pooled p=0.023, stage-combination p~0.08; median per-problem effect +0.045). Repulsion raises construction-hash diversity in eight of nine problems (one-sided p=0.0039; partly a manipulation check). The factorial finds no positive memory-by-repulsion interaction (bounded to about +/-0.04); the gain decomposes additively, and memory+repulsion is the only arm that never collapses (0 of 18 runs), within 0.025 of the full composition. A frontier proposer under the identical loop reaches in tens of samples what the local model does not in hundreds; in single scoping runs its gains arrive without the operators. The searches stall after closing 85-92% of the gap on the flagship problem, and a later analysis reads that plateau as a resolution limit: the reference value is a continuum limit and the unaided long-run finals already carry its family's structure. In the registered family-hint test the family named in words is adopted and loses; handed as code, it is optimized, but our best finite-grid encoding stays below the plateau reached unaided. We release the harness, every candidate, and the dated pre-registrations.
Software Engineering.comment: Version 4 of the paper (arXiv v2): adds the note on the wall (Zenodo v3) and corrections after an audit against the records (listed in the paper). 14 pages. Code: https://github.com/RobertoOno/interrupting-the-loop. Data: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22714138, 10.5281/zenodo.22713807 and 10.5281/zenodo.23163299; this version also at 10.5281/zenodo.23163677

Software Engineering.title: No Edges, No Verdict: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Declared Dependency Graphs in 78K SBOMs in the Wild
Software Engineering.summary: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) are consumed not only as component inventories but as dependency graphs: vulnerability triage, reachability filtering, and impact analysis all traverse the edges an SBOM declares. We present the first large-scale characterization of the declared dependency graph across 78,612 real-world SBOM files from the Wild SBOMs dataset (77,092 parseable). We find that the population splits into three regimes: 52.9% of SBOMs declare no edges at all (failing the NTIA minimum-elements requirement of dependency relationships; 42.3% once the 46.5% of files carrying the tool entry of a single generation harness are set aside), 8.8% declare a dependency block yet leave the majority of components isolated (degenerate regime; among such SBOMs with at least 50 components the median orphan share is 93%, and our 11 Syft-generated container-image SBOMs fall in this regime at 91.4-98.0% orphans), and 38.3% form well-connected graphs. Edge emission is predicted by the generator rather than by the format (0%-100% no-edge rates across tools), and the specification-level mechanism for declaring graph incompleteness (CycloneDX compositions) is used by 0.10% of CycloneDX documents. We argue that in the first two regimes, the common consumer inference "no path implies unreachable" is an unsound closed-world conclusion drawn from a demonstrably incomplete artifact; in a production vulnerability-prioritization system, replacing the resulting veto with an explicit "unknown" level guarded by a degeneracy detector recovered KEV recall from 0.600 to 0.950 (controlled re-scoring; 0.957 in a live end-to-end run) without alert flooding. The streaming scanner and the full per-SBOM topology dataset are archived on Zenodo.
Software Engineering.comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. v3: corrects the attribution of the "Github Extractor" documents (Fortress Information Security, not GitHub), reports results without the generation harness that produced 46.5% of the corpus, and links the code and data records

Software Engineering.title: Tracing Hallucinations in LLM Reasoning for UML Class Diagram Generation: An Empirical Taxonomy and Mitigation Study
Software Engineering.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate UML class diagrams from natural language requirements, but hallucinations may compromise the correctness and completeness of the resulting diagrams. Existing evaluations mostly assess the final diagram, without examining the intermediate traces of reasoning-capable LLMs, which can reveal where these hallucinations arise. We develop an empirical taxonomy of eleven hallucination sub-types organised into three dimensions: Prompt Faithfulness (deviations between requirements and reasoning), Code Faithfulness (discrepancies between reasoning and generated PlantUML code), and Reasoning Quality (problems within the reasoning). The taxonomy was derived from 60 manually annotated DeepSeek-R1 traces, applied to 120 further DeepSeek-R1 traces through a dual-LLM annotation pipeline, and examined on 20 DeepSeek-V4-Pro traces. Code Faithfulness was the most frequent dimension for DeepSeek-R1 in both datasets, whereas Prompt Faithfulness dominated for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, suggesting model-dependent failure patterns. In the manually annotated traces, reasoning-trace length showed no significant monotonic association with hallucination frequency, whereas requirement complexity was negatively associated with it, particularly for Prompt Faithfulness errors. In a mitigation experiment on 13 Golden UML ModelSet cases with three Qwen3-based models, adding Prompt Faithfulness and Reasoning Quality constraints to the generation prompt raised the pooled mean F1 score by 4.0 percentage points, whereas a post-hoc Code Faithfulness review provided no consistent further benefit. Relationship modelling remained the lowest-scoring element throughout. These results suggest that localising hallucinations within the generation process can inform targeted, prompt-based mitigation. Whether these findings generalise beyond the DeepSeek and Qwen3 model families remains to be tested.

Software Engineering.title: REGATTA: A Cross-Domain Measurement Framework and Fault-Injection Harness for Enterprise AI Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Enterprise AI-agent evaluation needs evidence about whether test suites expose specified faults and whether their reference rules are trustworthy. We introduce REGATTA (Regulatory Evaluation of Agents via Two-stage Testing and Assurance), a measurement framework with three instruments. A 125-item source-cited checklist spans five industry-by-jurisdiction cells across the United States and Vietnam. A 25-fault corpus covers five categories, and a harness scores suite-level fault detection at the design and execution stages. We examine four measurement diagnostics on 180 generated suites (5,400 scenarios) from three LLM generators. A source audit finds 24 items misstating the rule in force, 46 additional citation defects, 31 items with only non-binding, unidentifiable, or unverifiable sources, and 24 verified clean. Only initially substance-flagged items received author review; all 24 clean rows received AI review only. Results therefore describe the instruments as written, not legal compliance. Item coverage varies, execution-stage fault profiles are stable across generators, and the historical stages agree on $66$--$69\%$ of fault--suite pairs. A current-model US-insurance retest finds stage disagreement above repeated-execution variation, but stage agreement $.536$ falls below pooled chance $.549$, failing V3's lower inequality. Blind adjudication by one expert supports the design-stage judging protocol ($κ=.72$, 95% interval $[.52,.88]$); 40 current-model execution probes give $κ=.75$. The instruments, audit, and reusable code are released.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication at 2026 IEEE ICoDSE. 6 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Shares the historical experimental corpus and two-stage evaluation approach with arXiv:2606.04037; this paper focuses on measurement diagnostics and source audit, with a current-model retest and judge validation. Research artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23006005

Software Engineering.title: When Code Gets Cheap, Evaluation Gets Scarce: An Experience Report on AI-Assisted Agile Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Coding assistants are widely reported to speed up code production; most accounts stop there. We report the end-to-end construction and deployment of a compliance-critical, human-in-the-loop exam-grading system, built by a single developer who wrote no code by hand, protected by a gated process from stakeholder persona to audited behavior. The initial system was built in three working days and could grade a real cohort. We draw one claim from this experience: AI changes software engineering less by making programming faster than by changing what is scarce. Writing code becomes abundant. Reliable evaluation-knowing whether a result is correct and meets the actual need-remains necessary at every iteration and becomes the binding constraint. Engineering judgment remains a second scarcity. Several defects passed the test suite: they sat at the boundaries the tests had mocked, the browser and the language-model API, or appeared only in real use. Deployment exposed assumptions that local tests had missed. Moreover, an AI assistant acting across many steps bypassed process checkpoints until we made them enforceable gates. All of this was observed in a triple union: the developer was also the end user and domain expert, making expert judgment immediately available and evaluation as cheap as it can be. This favors the iteration gains, which may shrink where evaluation requires additional people or expertise, but makes the case a hard test for evaluation scarcity: evaluation still constrained progress. We draw five lessons: run a gated, traceable construction process; specify what is knowable and discover the rest against a running prototype; validate in the real environment; gate the assistant, not only the work; record decisions with their assumptions and the process state the assistant forgets. A second project showed similar patterns; an independent single-expert case corroborates the shift.

Software Engineering.title: ATLAS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Lifting Binary to Canonical Compiler IR
Software Engineering.summary: Lifting stripped, heavily optimized binaries to a canonical, pre-optimization LLVM intermediate representation (IR) is essential for downstream security analysis and legacy software migration when source code is unavailable. However, aggressive compiler optimizations rewrite control and data flow, remove structural metadata, and introduce type-erased low-level idioms, causing current lifters to produce malformed or semantically divergent IR. We present ATLAS, a multi-agent framework designed to reconstruct formally valid and canonical LLVM IR from optimized disassembly.ATLAS combines (i) Structure-aware, region-level retrieval, which utilizes pseudo-probe attribution to align optimized instructions with canonical IR exemplars, and (ii) a collaborative refinement loop that closes the gap between probabilistic generation and deterministic compiler constraints. Concretely, a Lift agent generates an initial IR draft conditioned on retrieved exemplars, an Advisor agent interprets LLVM verifier/compilation diagnostics and static checks to propose localized repair actions, and a Validation agent applies the edits, re-runs toolchain verification and (when available) runtime checks, and feeds the resulting diagnostics back to the Advisor. The agents iterate until the IR is verifier-clean and behaviorally consistent, or a budget limit is reached. On HumanEval-Decompile and MBPP, ATLAS outperforms seven baselines on lifting LLVM IR, achieving 91.8% re-executability and 89.4% CFG similarity across ARM, x86-64, and RISC-V binaries. Moreover, our evaluation demonstrates that ATLAS also outperforms the Binary to C to IR pipelines in pointer-flow precision and downstream analyzability. By recovering a well-formed, machine-centric representation, ATLAS enables practical cross-ISA recompilation and verifiable binary-only migration workflows.

Software Engineering.title: Separate Field Scoring Protects Unused Tools When Agents Pool Tool-Use Experience
Software Engineering.summary: Agents that call tools from a shared catalog can pool what they learn about which tool serves which request. We measure what pooled usage examples do to tool retrieval, reporting separately the held-out tools, for which no agent has usage, and all other tools. Adding usage examples to the index as extra entries for used tools raises Hit@5 (whether a gold tool is in the top five) for those tools and lowers it for held-out tools, by a large margin on two of three catalogs and with both embedders we tested. Giving used tools the same number of equally long entries filled with other tools' text lowers held-out Hit@5 about as much, but gives little or none of the gain. We call our method of scoring usage as its own field SYNAPSE. On StableToolBench, the held-out gold tool appears in its top five more often than with a router that reserves slots for usage (0.785 against 0.683), and this held-out lead holds on all three catalogs with both embedders. This protection persisted when we replaced each tool's usage with other tools' text, and a constant score offset for tools with usage gives similar held-out Hit@5 in most settings. The gain for tools with usage, in contrast, needs usage about the right tool. The router keeps more of the gain on labeled queries on TOUCAN with both embedders and on ToolRet with one, so the better choice depends on the workload. Splitting the usage among ten simulated agents shows that pooling helps exactly as much as giving one agent the same records.

Software Engineering.title: Measuring the Permission Gate: A Stress-Test Evaluation of Claude Code's Auto Mode
Software Engineering.summary:
Claude Code's auto mode is the first deployed permission system for AI coding agents, using a two-stage transcript classifier to gate dangerous tool calls. Anthropic reports a 0.4% false positive rate and 17% false negative rate on production traffic. We present the first independent evaluation of this system on deliberately ambiguous authorization scenarios, i.e., tasks where the user's intent is clear but the target scope, blast radius, or risk level is underspecified. Using AmPermBench, a 128-prompt benchmark spanning four DevOps task families and three controlled ambiguity axes, we evaluate 253 state-changing actions at the individual action level against oracle ground truth.
  Our findings characterize auto mode's scope-escalation coverage under this stress-test workload. The end-to-end false negative rate is 81.0% (95% CI: 73.8%-87.4%), substantially higher than the 17% reported on production traffic, reflecting a fundamentally different workload rather than a contradiction. Notably, 36.8% of all state-changing actions fall outside the classifier's scope via Tier 2 (in-project file edits), contributing to the elevated end-to-end FNR. Even restricting to the 160 actions the classifier actually evaluates (Tier 3), the FNR remains 70.3%, while the FPR rises to 31.9%. The Tier 2 coverage gap is most pronounced on artifact cleanup (92.9% FNR), where agents naturally fall back to editing state files when the expected CLI is unavailable. These results highlight a coverage boundary worth examining: auto mode assumes dangerous actions transit the shell, but agents routinely achieve equivalent effects through file edits that the classifier does not evaluate.

Software Engineering.title: PosterHarness: Turning Scientific Poster Generation into an Auditable Instruction-Following Benchmark
Software Engineering.summary: Text-rich image models can now design poster-scale layouts, but we lack ways to measure whether they honor scientific communication contracts: legible labels, prescribed aspect ratios, and -- above all -- abstaining from fabricated scientific figures. We present POSTERHARNESS, an auditable harness reframing poster generation as measurable instruction-following tasks, with a pilot benchmark and failure taxonomy. POSTERHARNESS uses a placeholder-first contract to separate two jobs models otherwise conflate. The model performs visual-summary design: typography, reading path, color, and background -- but never draws data-bearing figures. Every figure region must be an empty labeled placeholder; a deterministic compositor inserts real source-paper figures at detected coordinates. This makes properties measurable: placeholder count and ID accuracy, blankness, aspect-ratio compliance, abstention from synthesized graphics, public-text hygiene, and source-figure provenance -- with failures logged as explicit rejections, not hidden in plausible-looking output. We instantiate the harness on 12 papers (6 HEP, 6 AI/ML-adjacent) and report three findings. (i) A counterfactual probe shows the placeholder contract drives VLM-counted synthesized figures from 34 to 0 across three papers. (ii) A failure taxonomy identifies blocking contracts: placeholder geometry, placeholder QA, template critic, and public text. (iii) Comparison with Paper2Poster shows a trade-off: PosterHarness yields higher-resolution artifacts, lower white-canvas fraction, and stronger VLM visual preference; the deterministic baseline retains slightly more PosterQuiz-style information and runs faster. We report this as regime characterization, not a superiority claim. All artifacts, prompts, manifests, and audit scripts are released as a reusable evaluation component.

Software Engineering.title: What Ethereum Developers Ask For, and Whether They Get It: Ten Years of Ethereum Stack Exchange
Software Engineering.summary:
The Ethereum community learns where developers struggle through surveys and interviews, which record what developers say when asked about a chosen theme. Ethereum Stack Exchange (ESE) records what they ask for unprompted, and whether anyone resolves it. We study every question posted to ESE from Jan 2016 to Dec 2025, 54,637 in all, and label each with a prompt-based topic pipeline seeded with eight Ethereum-specific topics and open to new ones (22 topics in all). A three-provider committee of language models screens the labels, and manual adjudication of every disputed case puts their accuracy at 87.9 to 93.5%. Because the corpus is the complete record, no rate carries sampling error. We ask what developers ask for help with, whether the venue still resolves it, and, where it does not, whether the questions changed or their resolution did.
  Demand is concentrated on writing, deploying, and debugging contracts; the toolchain is the second-largest topic and growing, while security, consensus, and scaling are thin. Supply has weakened, and unevenly: answers still arrive, closure falls further. Across five estimators of the decade, the share of questions drawing any answer fell by 9.5 to 18.6 percentage points, but among answered questions the share reaching an accepted answer fell by 16.2 to 24.5. Rebuilding the later acceptance rate at the earlier topic mix moves the fall only from 9.40 to 9.32 points, so the topic mix does not explain it. Who asks separates outcomes far more sharply than what is asked: acceptance runs from 19.8% for askers below 10 reputation to 66.8% at 10k and above, a 47- point spread with a gradient in every year, against 17 across topics, and a shift toward newer askers accounts for up to 59% of the acceptance fall. The largest of seven properties an asker controls accompanies 5 points. The record places the support gap in the toolchain and among newcomers.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages, Mining Software Repositories

Software Engineering.title: VLTest: Finding Joint Image-Text Failures in Vision-Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. Mutating either input can change the expected answer, so an output change is not by itself a failure. Some failures appear only when both inputs are mutated; attributing them to the combination requires testing each mutation alone. We present VLTest, a black-box VLM testing approach. It generates image variants by editing VQGAN latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, filters variants likely to change the expected answer, and tests each variant alone before testing combinations, so every joint failure has four matched cells. A VLM judge confirms a failure only after checking that the input keeps the expected answer. On three tasks with eight VLMs, including two commercial API models, the oracle confirms 81.7% of the candidates, with 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates. Under the same budget, VLTest's generators find 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as SINVAD and TextFooler, and its joint tests find 91 to 197 attributed joint failures per 1,000 joint calls, 1.3 times as many as the same pairing applied to the baselines' variants.

Software Engineering.title: Trace2World: Reconstructing App Worlds from Real Interaction Traces for Scalable GUI Agent Training
Software Engineering.summary: Scaling GUI reinforcement learning requires environments that preserve real-app behavior. Yet coupling behavior inference with coding can turn partial traces into runnable mocks with incorrect state transitions. We introduce \textbf{Trace2World}, which separates global behavior reconstruction from implementation. It reconciles traces into a shared, source-linked app model, then compiles an executable environment. Independent replay of source workflows localizes mismatches for bounded implementation repair. Validated worlds then support learner-adaptive task and environment augmentation within source-supported behavior. From 1,570 traces, Trace2World constructs 50 environments. On 200 workflows across ten apps, 91.1% are reproduced end to end, versus 59.8% for the strongest matched task-local baseline. Source-grounded validation retains 94.0% of simulated training gains on real devices, versus 54.7% under self-validation. Learner guidance raises benchmark success from 56.9% to 61.1%. Training in Trace2World further improves the model by 20.2 points on our benchmark, 5.4--16.2 points across four external GUI benchmarks, and 16.3 points on 100 real-device tasks. Reliable reconstruction separates what behavior source evidence supports from whether the implementation preserves it.
Software Engineering.comment: Preprint. Under review

Software Engineering.title: Can Loan Processors and Underwriters Spot AI-Edited Statements? An Empirical Study
Software Engineering.summary: AI-assisted editing can produce loan documents that preserve familiar issuer layouts while changing the applicant's identity. We investigated whether experienced underwriters and loan processors identify such forgeries in first-pass, document-only review. Three practitioners recruited through Upwork each received one applicant package drawn from 134 forged PDFs derived from 47 genuine financial documents supplied with full consent. The edits preserved amounts, dates and balances; identifier inconsistencies introduced by the pipeline were knowingly retained before distribution. Reviewers were not told that files had been altered and returned 132 file-level judgements. Checking their explanations against the originals yielded 14 edit-supported concerns (10.6%): 12 Suspicious judgements and two Insufficient information judgements. All supported concerns involved identifier disagreements within or across documents, and no reported visual cue identified an actual edit. Thus, approximately one in ten judgements contained evidence of the forgery, despite known inconsistencies remaining in the files. These observations motivate evaluating consistency checks and independent source verification alongside human review. With three reviewer-package pairs and no genuine-file controls, the findings describe this exploratory setting rather than population-wide detection accuracy.
Software Engineering.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures

Software Engineering.title: Compositional Safety Failures in Harness Evolution: Identification and Runtime Monitoring
Software Engineering.summary: Self-evolving agent harnesses continually update persistent components such as memory, prompts, skills, and tools. We call this process harness evolution. However, such evolution could introduce unexpected safety risks. Existing work studies harness misevolution and validates candidate harnesses or attributed individual component updates, leaving safety analysis of cross-component update interactions largely unexamined. To address this gap, we study compositional safety failures in harness evolution, where interactions among individually safe and utility-preserving component updates can produce undesirable or unsafe agent behavior, revealing a safety risk intrinsic to harness evolution. Across three safety-related benchmarks, we identify 43 pairwise and 18 irreducible 3-way compositional safety failures. Conventional solution incurs combinatorial complexity in validating cross-component interactions, leaving the safety checking impractical as the harness evolves. To solve this, we introduced a typed hypergraph that represents component states as nodes and safety-relevant higher-order interactions as hyperedges. When the harness changes, the hypergraph updates only the interaction neighborhood of the changed states rather than reconstructing the global composition space. Building on that, we develop a hypergraph-guided runtime monitoring mechanism. Experiments show that our method effectively mitigates compositional safety risks while preserving task utility and reducing interaction-checking costs, and further reveal an empirical safety-utility-cost trade-off across different safety mechanisms.

Software Engineering.title: From Natural Language to Verified C: Verification-Guided Generation with ACSL Specifications
Software Engineering.summary: AI-assisted code generation amplifies the demand for automated formal verification. Generated programs must not only be executable but also accompanied by machine-checkable evidence of correctness. Existing approaches can synthesize functionally plausible code or plausible-looking specifications from natural-language prompts; however, they do not explicitly co-design the implementation and specification as a unified artifact optimized for verification. Consequently, automated verifiers often fail to discharge proof obligations. Typical failure modes include missing or implicit proof anchors, program structures that are hostile to automated reasoning, and inconsistencies between code-level state and specification-level requirement facts arising from the independent generation of code and specifications. Even when verification succeeds, it may only establish weak specifications that omit requirement-critical behavior. This paper introduces VeriGen-C, a formal-verification-friendly framework for the joint synthesis of C programs and ACSL specifications from natural-language requirements. Code generation and repair are constrained to expose proof-relevant state, to streamline control flow for deductive verification, and to eliminate implementation patterns that hinder automated proof search. Specification generation and refinement are similarly constrained to mitigate verification timeouts and to ensure alignment with the user requirements. Empirical evaluations on HumanEval-X, FM-Bench, and LiveCodeBench Lite demonstrate that VeriGen-C substantially improves the rate of verified and requirement-aligned solutions relative to an interface-compatible baseline, from 5.5% to 44.5%, from 44.3% to 80.0%, and from 6.5% to 58.7%, respectively.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables

Software Engineering.title: From Tokens to Credits to Outcomes: Pricing AI Across Models, Applications, and Cloud Platforms
Software Engineering.summary: Between 2023 and 2026, AI changed how software is priced. Traditional SaaS charged per seat because serving one more user cost almost nothing. Model inference has non-zero marginal cost, and usage varies by orders of magnitude across customers, producing prepaid credits, metered usage, hybrid seat-plus-usage models, and outcome pricing that supplement, and in rare cases replace, seat-based pricing. These pricing models have not been systematically characterized. This paper presents a reproducible study of public pricing artifacts - pricing pages and documentation - across three cohorts: the full Forbes AI 50 (2026) as the AI-native core sample, cloud platforms selling AI services included by a documented rule, and a frozen purposive cohort of 9 distinctive designs. It contributes (1) a dataset coding each offering's pricing primitive and credit mechanics with dated primary sources, prepared for public release with the paper, (2) a taxonomy of the primitives in use and their distribution across cohorts, and (3) empirically grounded requirements for automated, configurable billing platforms, including ledger state for credits, attribution pipelines for outcome pricing, and configuration support for high pricing-change velocity. Subscription with usage quota is the dominant observable model among AI-native companies (55% of observable AI-native rows; 45-61% under sensitivity analysis of hybrid boundary cases). 23 of the 52 AI-native rows publish no pricing. Hybrid products are better understood as compositions of packaging anchor, allowance mechanism, and billable unit than as mutually exclusive categories. All artifacts are public; my employer is excluded from the sample.
Software Engineering.comment: 25 pages

Software Engineering.title: Governance-State Corruption in Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents: A Cross-Model Stress Test
Software Engineering.summary: An LLM agent can retrieve a memory correctly yet use it incorrectly after its validity state changes. We study governance-state corruption: faults that alter which retained records enter model-visible context while stored content and tasks remain fixed. Across six providers, 731 benchmark-grounded bases yield 2,080 matched fault pairs. In offline control-plane checks, corruption changes the operative projection in 96.25% of pairs, while oracle-backed enforcement restores it in 100%. For downstream evaluation, a deterministically selected, non-probability LongMemEval/Memora panel resolves 298 of 300 matched triplets (238 distinct bases). Clean-minus-corrupted contrasts are 40.54 percentage points in LongMemEval binary correctness (95% base-cluster interval [30.32, 50.71]) and 30.60 points in rescaled Memora FAMA ([23.31, 37.69]); both sources also show recovery. OAKS Novel native option parity holds for all 6,714 resolved outputs. Full-cohort frozen-scorer corruption/recovery effects (-27.55/+27.51 points) remain descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects. These bounded findings motivate evaluating memory control-state integrity alongside retrieval accuracy.
Software Engineering.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 10 tables

Software Engineering.title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
Software Engineering.summary: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution

Software Engineering.title: Model of Things (MoT): A Model-Driven Approach to Streamline Cloud-of-Things Application Development
Software Engineering.summary: The convergence of Cloud Computing and the Internet of Things (IoT) underpins modern, scalable, and data-intensive systems. Cloud-of-Things (CoT) applications are now pervasive across healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation. Nevertheless, their development remains fragmented and technically demanding. Current CoT development approaches require substantial expertise in heterogeneous platforms, protocols, and deployment technologies. They offer limited model-driven support, weak automation, and poor alignment with low-code principles. As a result, developing CoT applications remains effort-intensive and error-prone. This study aims to simplify CoT application development by introducing the Model of Things (MoT). MoT integrates UML-based modeling with low-code execution concepts to reduce technical barriers while preserving automation and deployment feasibility. We designed a custom UML profile comprising nine CoT-specific stereotypes and an automated transformation pipeline. MoT was evaluated using one end-to-end case study and a Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) questionnaire with 12 participants with software modeling experience. In the evaluated case study, MoT generated executable application components from UML models, while users supplied the required configuration parameters and deployment settings. TAM results indicate strong acceptance: all 12 participants rated MoT positively for usefulness and ease of use, and qualitative feedback emphasized reduced complexity and faster development. MoT demonstrates that combining UML modeling with low-code execution is feasible and valuable for CoT systems. By enabling executable models and lowering entry barriers, MoT advances practical, model-driven CoT engineering and opens avenues for broader industrial adoption.
Software Engineering.comment: 38 pages, 23 figures, 7 tables

Software Engineering.title: Stale Instruction Files Override the Code in Coding Agents: A One-Sentence Fix
Software Engineering.summary:
Purpose: Coding agents follow a project's instruction file, such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, even when it disagrees with the existing code and even when they notice the disagreement. We measure this behaviour and test whether one sentence in the user's own instruction file makes agents follow the code instead.
  Methods: We built 40 Python projects in which the instruction file asks for one convention while the existing code uses another, for example print instead of logging. Claude Code and Codex CLI added a feature to each project, with and without a sentence in the user-level instruction file that gives the existing code precedence, in 320 runs.
  Results: Without the sentence, 90.1% of the agents' choices followed the stale file. Claude Code pointed out the conflict in 79 of 80 runs and still followed the file. Codex CLI rewrote the existing code to match the file in 20 of 80 runs, and the project's own tests then failed in 17 of them. The sentence raised the share of choices that follow the code from 4.2% to 91.4%, stopped the rewrites and raised the test pass rate from 89.4% to 100%.
  Conclusion: We attribute the behaviour to how agents receive the two sources: the instruction file reaches the model as an instruction and the code as tool output, which models are trained to rank lower. Users can add the sentence today, and makers of agents and models can build the same rule into their products.
Software Engineering.comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to SN Computer Science. Data and code: https://github.com/WenJing95/stale-docs-data

Software Engineering.title: Contextual Memory Virtualisation: DAG-Based State Management and Structurally Lossless Trimming for LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: As large language models engage in extended reasoning tasks, they accumulate significant state -- architectural mappings, trade-off decisions, codebase conventions -- within the context window. This understanding is lost when sessions reach context limits and undergo lossy compaction. We propose Contextual Memory Virtualisation (CMV), a system that treats accumulated LLM understanding as version-controlled state. Borrowing from operating system virtual memory, CMV models session history as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with formally defined snapshot, branch, and trim primitives that enable context reuse across independent parallel sessions. We introduce a three-pass structurally lossless trimming algorithm that preserves every user message and assistant response verbatim while reducing token counts by a mean of 20% and up to 86% for sessions with significant overhead by stripping mechanical bloat such as raw tool outputs, base64 images, and metadata. A single-user case-study evaluation across 76 real-world coding sessions demonstrates that trimming remains economically viable under prompt caching, with the strongest gains in mixed tool-use sessions, which average 39% reduction and reach break-even within 10 turns. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/IngressionLabs/contextual-memory-virtualisation.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages. 6 figures. Introduces a DAG-based state management system for LLM agents. Evaluation on 76 coding sessions shows up to 86% token reduction (mean 20%) while remaining economically viable under prompt caching. Includes reference implementation for Claude Code

Software Engineering.title: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: A durable agent can resume a consequential action while its authority changes and the action's external outcome remains uncertain. We study execution-time reliability of tool-using AI agents, isolating recovery decisions from language-model behavior. Checkpoint state, permission to dispatch, evidence of an external effect and permission to reconcile are distinct obligations. We present a finite conformance study that checks these obligations through histories scored against a provider effect ledger hidden from the recovering application. A prospectively frozen campaign executes 336 histories on native LangGraph and Temporal hosts, crossing 14 schedules, three provider contracts and four matched application policies. All 168 paired host cells have identical checked outcomes. Per host, retained-ledger reconciliation passes all 42 histories: 21 checked completions, 15 denials and six unknown outcomes with reservations retained. Cached retry, revalidation before retry and stable-key retry pass 30, 36 and 31 histories respectively. A separate 16-case component study of InfinityOS, an enterprise AI platform developed by Arya.ai, exercises exported authority, worker, recovery and settlement code over repository fakes. The results isolate the roles of current authority, provider contracts and retained observations in recovery, with safety, completion and unresolved obligations reported separately for the declared application profile.
Software Engineering.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables

Software Engineering.title: Knowing When to Stop: The Evidence-Action Gap in Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents are trained to complete tasks, and they keep trying even when the environment makes completion impossible. The evidence that only outside help can restore progress usually appears within a few steps, yet agents rarely act on it: they over-persist, attempt undesired workarounds, and claim success the record does not support -- a phenomenon we call evidence-action gap. To measure it, we introduce ImpasseBench, which injects twelve realistic environment blockers into otherwise solvable repair tasks and marks, in each trajectory, the step at which the collected evidence becomes sufficient. Scoring actions relative to that step separates appropriate effort from over-persistence and premature handoff. Across eight frontier models and 19,371 trajectories, we find that nearly every run that needs outside help collects sufficient evidence, yet a third still exhaust their budget, and every unsafe request we detect comes after that point. Fortunately, an escalation tool, or an external monitor for models that ignore the tool, already guards against much of this behavior: the tool cuts budget exhaustion from 34.0% to 6.7%, and the monitor nearly triples task success after environment restoration. Even then, a fired escalation is not yet a useful handoff: tickets reliably name the blocker but often omit the agent's own progress and verification status. Taken together, we argue that knowing when to stop therefore needs explicit support, both in the tool that lets an agent hand off and in the report it leaves behind.
Software Engineering.comment: 36 pages

Software Engineering.title: Loop Engineering: Building Blocks, Adoption, and Impact
Software Engineering.summary: Over the past months, the way developers guide agentic AI coding tools has moved up several levels of abstraction, from phrasing prompts to engineering context to configuring the harness around the underlying model. In June 2026, practitioners began to describe a new level called loop engineering: Instead of prompting an agent interactively, developers design systems that prompt agents for them. The term spread rapidly, accompanied by bold claims and vocal skepticism, but its adoption in software projects has not yet been measured. We present (1) an exploratory review of the emerging gray literature on loop engineering, (2) a traceability analysis and an exploratory mining study of 36,710 software repositories, and (3) the design of a controlled experiment to study how loop goals, static analysis checks, and decision policies affect task success, code quality, resource usage, and token consumption of agent loops. Our literature review found broad agreement on what a well-engineered loop contains: agent loops started on a schedule or by repository events and bounded by machine-checkable stop conditions, persistent state files, verifier subagents, token budgets, and defined points of escalation to humans. These sources provide no systematic evidence of the claimed benefits. In the mining study, we found autonomous agent loops in 217 open-source GitHub repositories using heuristics and behavioral signals. Nearly all of these repositories committed the configuration that starts their loops, but almost none of them committed the state files that the gray literature suggests. Our proposed experiment is a first step toward closing the evidence gap identified in our literature review. We call for further empirical studies of the benefits and costs of loop engineering for software engineering tasks.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 2 tables, 1 figure, 2nd Journal Ahead Workshop (JAWs@ASE 2026)

Software Engineering.title: The Influence of Code Smells in Efferent Neighbors on Class Stability
Software Engineering.summary: Understanding what drives code instability is essential for effective software maintenance, as unstable classes require larger or more frequent edits and increase the risk of unintended side effects. Although code smells are widely believed to harm maintainability, most prior stability studies examine only the smells within the class being modified. In practice, however, a class can change because its efferent neighbors (i.e., the classes it depends on) are modified due to ripple effects that propagate along static dependencies, even if the class itself is clean. Such ripple effects may be more severe when efferent neighbors exhibit code smells. Therefore, this study investigates whether code smells in a class's efferent neighbors affect its stability. We mined one year of commit history from 152 top-starred GitHub Java projects, detected code smells and static dependencies, and modeled their associations with class stability. Our results challenge the practice of examining code smells only within the class being maintained by showing that this provides an incomplete view of stability risk. Specifically, considering code smells in efferent neighbors reveals stability risks that are not observed when examining code smells in the class itself. Moreover, considering smells in both the class and its efferent neighbors, as well as their relationships across dependencies, reveals further stability risks that are not observed when smells at these two locations are analyzed separately. Consequently, these findings suggest that code smell analysis for class maintenance should extend beyond the class being maintained to the classes on which it depends.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted as a Registered Report at the International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR) 2026. Stage 2 submission under review at Empirical Software Engineering (EMSE)

Software Engineering.title: SWE-Clar: Can Coding Agents Clarify Incomplete Client Requirements and Deliver Greenfield Software?
Software Engineering.summary: Greenfield software development in freelance settings requires coding agents to turn incomplete client requests into working software. This makes requirement clarification essential, yet clients may be unable to provide continuous feedback over long development cycles, and receiving their answers does not guarantee correct understanding of complex requirements. These challenges motivate two benchmark design choices: clarification precedes code implementation, and its effectiveness is assessed through explicit tests of requirement understanding. Guided by these choices, we introduce SWE-Clar, a benchmark grounded in real, high-value client commissions to evaluate requirement clarification and code implementation in this setting. It comprises 100 tasks based on real software development jobs on Upwork, each with at least US\$4,000 in total payments. Each task begins with multi-round interaction between a coding agent and a client agent, followed by separate runs for code implementation with acceptance testing and clarification assessment. For the latter, we construct 512 questions paired with reference answers from real client-freelancer interactions, covering both explicitly stated requirements and those inferred from the conversational context. Both runs begin from the same clarification context but remain isolated, preventing assessment questions from guiding code implementation. Experiments with nine frontier models show that even GPT-6 Astra, which has the highest observed implementation score, achieves a task pass rate of only 67%, underscoring the challenge of independent software delivery in this setting. The dataset and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/upwork/SWE-Clar.
Software Engineering.comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/upwork/SWE-Clar

Software Engineering.title: Ulysses: A Security Harness For Synthesizing Verifiable Web Exploits
Software Engineering.summary: How can an AI agent automatically discover security vulnerabilities in any software repository? Existing approaches use LLMs to generate software vulnerability exploits. However, it is challenging for an LLM to reliably verify its own generated exploits. In this paper, we propose Ulysses, a multi-agent security harness to synthesize verifiable vulnerability exploits for web applications. Ulysses converts candidate vulnerability findings into verified Proofs of Exploitability by iteratively exploring exploit hypotheses and establishing success in independently observed execution effects. We evaluated Ulysses on WebExploitGym, a curated benchmark of exploitable instances from 25 real-world web applications that span 5 languages and 7 frameworks. Ulysses produces verified proofs for 10 of 25 real-world advisories. It also discovered 4 new proofs of exploitability that have never been previously reported.
Software Engineering.comment: 23 pages, 6 Figures

Software Engineering.title: CuraLoc: Repository-Level Fault Localization via Planned Code Inspection
Software Engineering.summary: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. Existing repository-level localization methods often let language models iteratively decide what code to inspect next, requiring repeated model calls and substantial token usage. We investigate whether these inspection decisions can instead be planned before source retrieval. In this research, we introduce CuraLoc, which first selects candidate files and represents their symbols using compact behavioral and structural descriptions. In a single planning decision, the model jointly selects starting symbols, chooses code relationships to inspect from each, and forms hypotheses about likely edits. Deterministic retrieval collects the requested source for a final ranking informed by those hypotheses, concentrating model reasoning on choosing and comparing code rather than directing each retrieval step. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on the SWE-Bench Lite and Verified datasets. On SWE Bench Verified with GPT-5.2, CuraLoc raises Func@1 from LocAgent's 53.8% to 59.3% while using 90.3% fewer recorded tokens, and also outperforms RepoSearcher (56.2%) and Agentless (39.6%) on Func@1. On SWE-bench Lite, CuraLoc achieves a high 83.8% Func@5 accuracy improving on Agentless by more than 15% in relative accuracy. Additionally, CuraLoc supports different model backbones, with strong localization accuracy demonstrated using both GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra. These results provide evidence that repository-level code inspection can be planned effectively without iterative model-controlled navigation.

Software Engineering.title: A Reduced Stochastic Model of Microservice Availability: Algorithms for Identification and Formal Analysis
Software Engineering.summary: Estimating microservice operation availability requires connecting runtime observations to completion of the required work within a deadline. Detailed architectural models provide one route, but their reconstruction and analysis can be costly. We present algorithms for identifying and analysing a reduced stochastic availability model from telemetry and declared operation requirements. The identification procedure constructs a joint law of execution states and retains compatible laws when observations are incomplete. Formal results establish attainable probability bounds and conditions for identifying a completion-and-deadline representation directly. This construction preserves the range obtained by evaluating the same completion-and-deadline event in the full model; a separate joint comparison describes the structural information discarded. An independent study covered three microservice applications and 18 campaigns. On complete common campaigns with point forecasts from both methods, observed mean absolute errors differed from those of independently extracted PMX/Palladio architectural models by at most 0.082 percentage points. The full graph-based workflow from telemetry to first forecast was 31.73-100.24 times faster than the studied PMX/Palladio workflow, including startup and launcher waits. Direct identification preserved the retained forecasts and intervals, with median paired first-answer savings of 5.1-11.2% relative to full execution-model analysis. The results connect required model detail to measured identification and analysis costs.

Software Engineering.title: Autoregressive Multimodal Anomaly Detection with Large Language Models for Microservice Systems
Software Engineering.summary: Microservice systems have become a dominant architecture for large-scale cloud applications, enabling rapid deployment and elastic scaling. However, ensuring the reliability and availability of microservice systems critically relies on effective anomaly detection, as failures and performance anomalies can quickly propagate across services and severely impact end-to-end system behavior. Existing multimodal anomaly detection approaches for microservice systems often struggle with two fundamental limitations: (i) the neglect of modality-specific characteristics in favor of cross-modality fusion, and (ii) the "identity-shortcut" problem that affects the feature reconstruction process. To address these issues, we propose LLMMAD, an autoregressive multimodal anomaly detection framework for microservice systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs). Initially, to reconcile cross-modality fusion with modality-specific preservation, LLMMAD embeds and recombines multimodal data into a unified sequence for LLM processing to model inter-modality relationships, while employing modality-wise reconstruction heads to retain modality-specific information. Subsequently, to eliminate the identity-shortcut, we implement a prediction-driven autoregressive objective, under which the model predicts future states rather than copies current inputs. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that LLMMAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving F1-score improvements of 3.1%, 1.4%, and 0.9%, respectively, thereby providing a more reliable solution for microservice monitoring.
Software Engineering.comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables

Software Engineering.title: What Open-Source Projects Tell Their Coding Agents: A Census of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents can be guided with instruction files in a repository. We examine this emerging practice through a census of popular, active GitHub repositories in thirteen languages, treating each repository's root AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md as one instruction set. Agent instructions appear in of repositories and of the most-starred; where both files exist, CLAUDE.md usually points to AGENTS.md. We analyse statements using model-assisted annotation and human review. The annotations reveal a practical mix of project knowledge and rules about code, building and workflow. Collaboration rules name concrete requirements, from test plans to commit formats, yet of directives give no reason. Projects disagree on AI attribution: commit-message rules more often prohibit it than require it, while pull-request rules more often require disclosure. A third of instruction sets have a generator-associated signature, a tool-inserted block, shared text or an AI-marked creation commit; four in five are edited after creation. Prespecified tests associate repository popularity with rules on pull requests and AI contributions. Exploratory analyses link activity to process-oriented content and show that LLM and agent projects are over-represented among adopters. The models agree much more closely with each other than with the human reviewer's topic assignments, a caution for automated annotation. We release the annotations, taxonomies and pointers to the analysed file versions.

Software Engineering.title: Reuse, Rewrite, or Reject: Evidence-Constrained Trace Reuse for Repeated Mobile GUI Control
Software Engineering.summary: Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.

Software Engineering.title: MBABench-2.0: Evaluating AI Agents on Constructing Financial Spreadsheets Beyond Simple Verifiability
Software Engineering.summary: Spreadsheets are the lingua franca of modern finance, driving valuation, forecast, audit, and many other core workflows of the industry. As LLM agents advance to automate knowledge work, spreadsheet construction is a natural and pertinent testbed. However, most existing spreadsheet benchmarks evaluate agents on fill-in-the-blank style tasks, where an agent performs minor edits in otherwise complete spreadsheets. This protocol fails to capture the most central and time-consuming part of the spreadsheet workflow: the modeling decisions, format design, and sheet layout regular knowledge workers need to toil through to build a workbook from scratch. We introduce MBABench-2.0, a benchmark of 101 original spreadsheet construction tasks, the hardest of which is estimated to take 33 hours for a modeler with 3+ years of experience. Unlike coding or math, where a unit test or a final answer can verify an agent's output, the quality of a financial spreadsheet that concerns readability, maintainability, or auditability, is not so simply verifiable. To holistically evaluate spreadsheet construction, we introduce 129 criteria spanning 12 categories that operationalize quality beyond the accuracy of the spreadsheet. Evaluating over 20 agents across 8 models and 4 harness types, we find that frontier agents rarely construct spreadsheets that are both accurate and meet our quality criteria: the top agent achieves a pass rate of only 16% on the benchmark. The benchmark demonstrates a substantial gap in spreadsheet building capability of current agents.

Software Engineering.title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction Costs Long-Horizon Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Context compaction lets long-horizon coding agents continue beyond their context windows, but can erase the state needed to finish a task. Prior evaluations measure efficiency, retained information, or end-to-end success, leaving the effect of a specific history replacement difficult to isolate. Compact-Bench pairs full-history and summary-only continuations from a shared repository state, and evaluates recurring details and successive production compactions. It covers 35 SWE-bench repairs, 146 agentic sessions, and 106 production chains. Across 14 summarizer backbones, stable damage ranges from 5-64% of 22 full-history successes: Claude Opus 4.8 preserves the most repairs, while DeepSeek-Flash damages the most. With Kimi-K3 as summarizer, the Kimi Code prompt preserves the most task continuations (19/22), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details (15.0%). LLM summaries retain at most 16.0% of recurring details, compared with 79.1% for mechanical extraction; production summaries retain 15.7% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13/14 backbones, and another by all 5 prompts. These results show that reliable compaction requires preserving the progress needed to complete a task, and that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful continuation. Code is available at https://github.com/cai-jianfeng/compact-bench and data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/caijanfeng/compact-bench.

Software Engineering.title: Mining the Design Space of Multi-Agent Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: Designing large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems (MAS) still relies on trial and error and informal "folk wisdom." Manual studies test only a few communication structures or topologies (e.g., sequential, parallel, shared-memory, or debate), while automated optimizers discard search trajectories after selecting a task-specific workflow. We present a two-phase pipeline for mining reproducible design principles from workflow code and execution traces. We repurpose AFlow's MCTS optimizer across six composable operators and 26 deterministically verified Enigmata tasks, retaining all intermediate rounds to build a corpus of 28,568 executable workflows. A sandboxed AutoResearch loop then mines orchestration code and prompt templates under an $L_0$-penalized validation objective and tests candidate principles on held-out searches. Across 300 feature-mining trials, we identify effects that persist on held-out searches across three levels of workflow design: workflows beginning with independent solvers and one-shot aggregation (Star-first) perform worse ($Δ= -0.045$); persistent shared documents (SharedMemory) outperform debate ($Δ= +0.135$); and prompt specificity and placeholder-based context routing yield gains comparable to communication-structure selection ($Δ= +0.118$). More broadly, our pipeline and results show the feasibility of turning discarded search trajectories into a statistical testbed for discovering and validating multi-agent workflow design principles.
Software Engineering.comment: 21 pages, including appendices. Equal contribution: Xavier Cadet and Junyan Cheng. Website: https://junyan.ch/apex-paper/

Operating Systems.title: uGDS: A User-Space Development Kit for High-Performance GPU Direct Storage
Operating Systems.summary:
Data-intensive GPU applications increasingly rely on NVMe SSDs to extend GPU memory. NVIDIA GPU Direct Storage (GDS) enables direct SSD-GPU transfers via PCIe peer-to-peer DMA, eliminating host staging. However, GDS retains three key limitations: (1) its control path traverses the kernel for every I/O request, introducing software overhead; (2) its stream-ordered path imposes strict total ordering even when workloads only require batch-level ordering; and (3) its closed-source user-space engine hinders diagnosis and custom scheduling.
  We present uGDS, https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS, an open-source user-space GPU Direct Storage library built on four principles: user-space control, unified cross-vendor abstraction, workload-aware scheduling, and end-to-end transparency. The host CPU manages the entire NVMe command lifecycle in user space, while payloads move via PCIe P2P DMA without consuming GPU compute. A minimal kernel module is used only for one-time privileged setup. uGDS partitions hardware queues between synchronous and batch traffic, enforces DMA-safe buffer lifetimes, and provides cuFile-compatible synchronous, batched, and stream-ordered APIs with polling or interrupt completion on both NVIDIA CUDA and AMD HIP.
  Evaluated on an A100 with a Samsung 990 PRO, uGDS achieves up to 12.12x GDS's batch-read bandwidth and 30.69x its batch-write bandwidth (8- and 4-KiB requests, batch size 128), and reduces 4-KiB synchronous write latency by 84.1% with two threads. Its stream-ordered path sustains 5.49 GiB/s on a single stream, where GDS retains only 40.8% of its synchronous bandwidth. In LMCache, uGDS reduces median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by up to 62.7% and raises serving goodput by 2.63x. On AMD, uGDS achieves up to 1.19x hipFile's synchronous-write bandwidth.
Operating Systems.comment: 17 pages,16 figures, Technical report. Source code: https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/uGDS

Performance.title: Cluster, Route, Escalate: Cascaded Framework for Cost-Aware LLM Serving
Performance.summary: Serving open-weight language models on premises forces a trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. Hosting models of different sizes lets easy queries go to a small, efficient model and hard ones to a large model. We present CRE-Router (Cluster, Route, Escalate), a two-stage method that decides which of these models answers each query. It clusters queries and routes each cluster to the model that best trades error against cost, under a budget on the time per output token (TPOT) or the end-to-end latency per request (E2EL). It then either accepts the answer or, when a quality estimator rejects it, escalates the query to the strong model. Routing decides before generation, so a hard query goes straight to the strong model; escalation decides after, so it can catch the errors routing cannot predict. It needs no annotation beyond task-correctness labels. We evaluate CRE-Router on TeleMath, TeleQnA and AIME, with pools of two to nine models served on A100 GPUs. CRE-Router is more accurate than the efficient models in its pool and comparable to the strong model it escalates to, at a lower cost per token. We also find that the choice of cost term decides which models serve the workload, that pricing each model per cluster shortens the wait per request, and that a change of hardware changes the best routing.
Performance.comment: Code: https://github.com/ymoslem/CRE-Router

Performance.title: Toward Open ISA Supercomputing: A Comparative Study of RISC-V, Arm, and x86 Architectures on HPC Workloads
Performance.summary: RISC-V is emerging as a candidate architecture for high-performance computing (HPC), but its competitiveness against established x86 and Arm processors remains difficult to assess because existing studies use different platforms, workloads, and methodologies, and rarely consider energy efficiency. Our work provides an evaluation of contemporary HPC RISC-V, Arm, and x86 processors using a common software stack and methodology. We characterize the Sophgo SG2044 and compare it with the NVIDIA Grace CPU Superchip and Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ across four HPC benchmarks (STREAM, HPL, HPL-MxP, and HPCG) and four representative applications (iPIC3D, PLUTO, OpenFOAM, and llama.cpp). The version of HPL-MxP linked to OpenBLAS built and used for this work is made available as open-source software. The SG2044 reaches 8.02 GFLOP/s of FP64 performance and 7.8 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core, increasing to 294 GFLOP/s and 107 GB/s at 64 cores. L2-cache-aware process placement enables near-linear scaling up to 16 cores, beyond which memory-bandwidth saturation limits further gains. Across generations of RISC-V hardware, in the context of the Monte Cimone (MC) project, the SG2044-based MCv3 doubles both single-core performance and peak memory bandwidth relative to MCv2, while improving memory bandwidth, node-level FP64 performance, and energy efficiency by approximately 100x, 158x, and 10x, over MCv1. Against the Arm and x86 systems, the SG2044 shows 8-15x less absolute performance, reflecting its narrower vector resources and less advanced technology node, but delivers competitive scaling and energy efficiency on several workloads. Its most notable result is LLM decode, where 64-core execution provides the highest relative scaling and energy efficiency among the evaluated platforms while exceeding Intel in throughput. Our results show that RISC-V processors are closing the gap with the competition.
Performance.comment: Preprint submitted to Future Generation Computer Systems

Performance.title: Measuring the Energy Cost of Completing Tasks with Quantized Language-Model Agents
Performance.summary:
Quantization reduces the memory and energy needed to serve large language models (LLMs) and AI agents for coding and data analysis can now run on locally hosted LLMs. In practice, this benefit is commonly benchmarked per output token. Yet an agent calls its model repeatedly, runs tools, and revises its work, and quantization can change both how much the agent generates and whether it succeeds. Existing energy studies either compare quantized models on single requests or measure agents at one fixed precision, overlooking how a change in precision plays out across a complete agent task.
  To address this gap, this paper presents the first characterization of the task-level energy trade-offs of model quantization in locally hosted agents. We develop 29 agent tasks with automatic pass/fail checks in six families, ranging from single-answer SQL analytics to multi-step repository bug fixing, and measure CPU and GPU energy per output token and per completed task for 4-bit and 8-bit versions of two open-weight models on bare-metal NVIDIA A100 nodes with llama.cpp.
  Our findings reveal that 4-bit precision generally saves energy per token, though whether it saves energy per completed task is task dependent and changes with the model and the execution budget (i.e., limits on turns, tokens, and time). We trace this discrepancy to the extra tokens needed to complete a task in full, which translates into using up to 3.5 times as much energy per completed task. These findings offer actionable guidance for developers and operators choosing model precision for agents, showing how tokens per completed task, set against the per-token saving, reveal whether lower precision completes the work with less energy.
Performance.comment: 26 pages, 7 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: Embodied Emissions of 2.5D and 3D Scaling in Chipletized GPUs for Low-Carbon AI
Hardware Architecture.summary: GPU compute resources are scaling to support growing AI workloads, leading to further rises in the climate change impact of hyperscale data centers that rely on high-performance GPUs. To model how packaging decisions impact the carbon footprint we have estimated the embodied emissions (EE) of a chiplet-based GPU that has been scaled in 2.5D and 3D using the imec.netzero modelling platform. We doubled the number of compute units and high bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity in the 2.5D and 3D scaled systems and found that 3D scaling results in an 89% increase in EE, as compared to an increase of 141% for 2.5D scaling, positioning 3D scaling as an attractive solution to limit the embodied emissions due to GPU scaling.

Hardware Architecture.title: Automated Multi-Line Bug Repair Using Model Checker Aided LLMs: A Case Study on RISC-V Processors
Hardware Architecture.summary: Functional verification of Register-Transfer Level(RTL) designs has become a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor development, often consuming the majority of project resources. Debugging, in particular, remains an especially time-consuming task, requiring careful analysis of simulation traces or counterexamples. Recent work has explored applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to RTL debug and repair with great promise. However, the existing approaches typically are for single-line bugs, operate in open-loop, rely heavily on prompts or retrieval, lack scalability, and often produce incorrect fixes. In this paper, we propose a novel automated RTL bug repair methodology that combines LLMs, assertions, and a model checker to provide scalable, trustworthy semantic grounding and formal guarantees. Concretely, the methodology leverages failing assertions to guide the LLM in generating patches for multi-line bugs. Each candidate patch is formally verified using a model checker (JasperGold), ensuring only valid repairs are accepted. We evaluate the efficacy and scalability of our methodology on the BRISC-V RISC-V core using mutation testing, introducing several mutation types, and demonstrate that our methodology can repair up to 98% of single-line RTL bugs and 93% of the multi-line bugs.
