The task involves jointly constructing expressive function specifications and their proofs, and ensuring that library interfaces compose along intended call sequences even without a designated client. We present Accord, an LLM-assisted framework for building machine-checked assurance cases: structured, auditable artifacts supporting the claim that a C codebase meets its intended requirements. To model intended cross-interface use in open libraries, Accord constructs an interface protocol that exposes permitted call sequences and resource assumptions for review, with a conditional safety guarantee under verified contracts and caller obligations. Accord coordinates two complementary phases: (i) requirement-guided analysis and bottom-up construction of candidate specifications and protocols; and (ii) modular proof construction with feedback that revises the specifications and proofs. Implemented using VST in Rocq, Accord establishes memory safety for 259 function definitions across seven implementation cases from six benchmark families, including industrial cryptographic modules, and additional functional correctness for red--black trees and ML-DSA. Human review took an estimated 0.17--8.00 hours per case. The guarantees depend on disclosed contracts and assumptions; human review supplies the conformance judgments connecting the formal artifacts to the intended requirements.
Software Engineering.comment: Substantially revised and expanded; updated title, formal development, and experimental evaluation

Software Engineering.title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
Software Engineering.summary: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.
Software Engineering.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables

Software Engineering.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

Software Engineering.title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
Software Engineering.summary: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.

Software Engineering.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
Software Engineering.summary: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

Software Engineering.title: Technology-Enabled Fuel Supply Chain Resilience: An Integrated Information System for Real-Time Monitoring and Decision Support
Software Engineering.summary: This study evaluates and extends the transactional information system described in an earlier fuel logistics study, focusing on data reliability, monitoring, and decision support. An author-led re-evaluation examined available Delphi and SQL code and compared a reconstructed source-derived baseline (R0) with a revised SQL Server system (R1) across twelve evaluation scenarios. Synthetic transactions and public US energy data were used for technical assessment, while organizational processes and supply delays were simulated. R1 improved data integration and reporting accuracy in controlled SQL Server tests and introduced stock-movement records, automated alerts, and recovery controls. On comparable data feeds, integration defect rates decreased from 2.90 to 3.46 percent in R0 to 0.14 to 0.49 percent in R1. For national weekly demand forecasting, selected methods did not significantly outperform the previous-year mean. Process and disruption simulations suggested improvements in manual workload and replenishment delays, although these outcomes depended on modelling assumptions and were not observed in operational settings. The study presents a revised transactional architecture for fuel logistics and distinguishes experimentally measured information-system performance from simulated organizational outcomes. Its findings highlight the potential of traceable inventory records, early exception detection, and recoverable information systems to support supply chain resilience.

Software Engineering.title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
Software Engineering.summary:
Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity.
  We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

Software Engineering.title: Model Compression vs. Adversarial Robustness: An Empirical Study on Language Models for Code
Software Engineering.summary: Transformer-based language models for code have shown remarkable performance in various software analytics tasks, but their adoption is hindered by high computational costs, slow inference speeds, and substantial environmental impact. Model compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation have gained traction in addressing these challenges. However, the impact of these strategies on the robustness of compressed language models for code in adversarial scenarios remains poorly understood. Understanding how these compressed models behave under adversarial attacks is essential for their safe and effective deployment in real-world applications. To bridge this knowledge gap, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of how common compression strategies affect the adversarial robustness of compressed models. We assess the robustness of compressed versions of three widely used language models for code across three software analytics tasks, using six evaluation metrics and four commonly used classical adversarial attacks. Our findings indicate that compressed models generally maintain comparable performance to their uncompressed counterparts. However, when subjected to adversarial attacks, compressed models exhibit significantly reduced robustness. These results reveal a trade-off between model size reduction and adversarial robustness, underscoring the need for careful consideration when deploying compressed models in security-critical software applications. Our study highlights the need for further research into compression strategies that strike a balance between computational efficiency and adversarial robustness, which is essential for deploying reliable language models for code in real-world software applications.

Software Engineering.title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
Software Engineering.summary: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.

Software Engineering.title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
Software Engineering.summary: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

Software Engineering.title: Behavioral Containment: Source-to-Binary Function Matching for 1-Day Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering.summary:
Vulnerabilities in reused open-source code often propagate into deployed binaries. Detecting them requires source-to-binary function matching, which locates the affected source function in a binary. Applying prior binary-to-binary approaches to this task would require compiling the source code with the same build configuration as the target binary, which is usually unavailable. Decompiling the binary does not make prior source-to-source approaches work either, because decompiled code differs substantially from the original source code.
  We observe that compilation transforms the code of a function but largely preserves its behavior. A binary function that implements a source function therefore contains its behavior, a property we call behavioral containment. Building on this, we present SBIND, which decompiles the binary and checks behavioral containment instead of comparing code. SBIND represents each function by behavioral paths, sequences of normalized operations from its entry to its exits, and aligns source paths with binary paths in order. To detect 1-day vulnerabilities, SBIND compares the binary with the vulnerable and the patched source only on the paths through the changed lines. On stripped binaries built with two compilers, two optimization levels, and four architectures, SBIND ranks the correct function first in 77.87% of 32,008 searches, against 45.69% for the state-of-the-art approach SBridge. On 26 1-day CVEs, SBIND reaches an F1 score of 0.70 on stripped binaries, against 0.51 for SBridge. Our replication of SBridge also revealed several issues in its implementation and evaluation, and its authors have acknowledged them.

Software Engineering.title: Distilling Reasoning Traces into Advisory Prompts for Software Engineering Tasks
Software Engineering.summary: Language models are widely used for generating and otherwise processing code (e.g., predicting behavior, outputs, or likely inputs), and this paper asks whether better performance can be achieved without always incurring the cost of reasoning. Human students of programming learn to avoid mistakes by (a) first identifying them, (b) reflecting upon cognitive lapses that led to these mistakes (essentially, "thinking through" the errors), (c) inferring general rules or lessons from these reflections, and (d) internalizing these lessons into rules. In tutorial sessions with an instructor, this is a very common Socratic interaction with students. Examples of such internalizable rules might include the nugget "Before coding, restate the requirements to clarify them". Inspired by this process, this paper describes an approach where we first identify examples in which "thinking mode" in a (low-resource) LLM avoids errors; then, these errors, and their avoidance via "thinking" in the same LLM, are examined by a bigger LLM to generate summary explanations; these are then summarized by a large LLM into brief advisory prompts. This approach works on many modestly sized models; in some cases, the "advisory prompts" thus learned can also be gainfully transferred to other models. We also present some investigations into the nature of coding errors that language models make, and a characterization of when this approach can be helpful.
